=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel – Buyer-side review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**To:** Wattlebridge deal team
**Status:** Privileged / draft advice. Based solely on the Seller's cover note and Disclosure Letter; the full SPA text has not been reviewed, so clause-level drafting points should be confirmed against the current SPA draft.

## 1. Headline view

The package is not "fair and balanced." Read against the Disclosure Letter, the Seller Update is in several places internally inconsistent: the cover note describes matters as "addressed," "adequate," "settled" or "not material," while the Seller's own Disclosure Letter (which is the operative document) confirms that none of the key open items has actually been resolved. That inconsistency is useful leverage and we should use it.

The structural problem is that the Seller is trying to do three things at once:

1. **Collapse every protection into one weak regime** – a 20% cap, 18-month window, excess-only basket, applied to *all* Claims (fundamental, tax, IP, specific indemnities included) unless expressly carved out.
2. **Neutralise warranties through disclosure** – general disclosure of the whole data room and public registers, plus a constructive-knowledge bar (cl. 8.3) that would defeat claims on anything "discoverable."
3. **Leave known, quantified liabilities in the Company** post-Completion while taking a price struck on a debt-free/cash-free basis.

Items 1 and 2 together mean that for the known problems (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonuses, DD-006, Sandbar) a warranty claim would be essentially impossible: they are disclosed, so warranties don't bite; they are "discoverable," so cl. 8.3 bars them; and even if a claim survived, the cap/basket/time limits apply. Those matters therefore have to be dealt with by **price, Completion deliverables, conditions and specific indemnities**, not warranties.

Roughly quantified, the identified items the Seller is proposing to leave with the Company or unaddressed are:

| Item | Amount | Seller's proposal | Effect on debt-free/cash-free price |
|---|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility | ~AUD 3,200,000 | Release "following Completion" | Buyer effectively pays this twice |
| DD-005 completion bonuses | AUD 420,000 + on-costs (super, payroll tax) ~AUD 500,000+ | Not in funds flow; "matter for Seller" | Company pays post-Completion |
| Ironquay SOW3 fee | AUD 180,000 (+ IP not yet vested) | Indemnity for the fee only | IP title risk unpriced |
| Sandbar renewals | AUD 330,000 | "Ordinary course" | Possibly unaccrued committed cost |
| **Total** | **~AUD 4.2m+ (c. 17% of price)** | | |

Plus unquantified exposure on Bluefen (~30% of revenue) and the DD-006 privacy incident.

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### 2.1 Liability regime (cl. 12.1–12.3, 13) – reject the "one regime for everything" approach

**Cap (20% / AUD 4.8m).** A 20% general-warranty cap is at the low end but within range for an Australian mid-market private deal; it is negotiable rather than unacceptable *provided* it applies only to general business warranties. We should open at a higher figure (30–50%) and may ultimately accept something in the 20–30% range if the carve-outs below are secured. Note also that if we take W&I insurance, the cap debate changes shape – worth raising with the brokers now.

**Fundamental/title warranties.** The Seller's proposal to subject capacity and title warranties to the same cap and 18-month limit "for administrative simplicity" is not market and must be rejected. If title to the shares fails, the Buyer has paid AUD 24m for nothing; a AUD 4.8m recovery capped at 18 months is no remedy. Position: fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, no insolvency, share capital) at 100% of price, with a 6–7 year (or statutory limitation) claim period, outside the de minimis and basket.

**Tax.** The Seller says tax is "settled under the general regime." It is not. ATO amendment periods run 4 years from assessment in most cases (longer for fraud/evasion and certain matters), so an 18-month window leaves the Buyer exposed for most of the audit period. Position: tax warranties and a stand-alone tax indemnity with a 7-year period, cap at 100% of price (or at minimum well above the general cap), not subject to disclosure, de minimis or basket.

**IP.** For an analytics business, IP is the asset. Given the known Ironquay defect (see 2.6), IP warranties should sit at an elevated cap (at least 50%, ideally 100%) with a longer period (e.g. 3–4 years), and should not be swept into the 18-month/20% regime.

**Thresholds.** De minimis of AUD 25,000 (~0.1%) is at the top of the usual range; AUD 10–15k is more typical for this deal size. Basket of AUD 250,000 (~1%) is market, but it should be a **tipping** basket (recover from the first dollar once exceeded), not excess-only. Related claims arising from the same facts should aggregate for de minimis purposes – the Sandbar structure (three contracts of AUD 110k each) shows exactly why.

**The "sweeper" (cl. 12.3 second sentence).** "Any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" is the most dangerous single line in the Update. On its face it subjects the Ironquay indemnity, any tax indemnity, leakage claims, completion-accounts adjustments, and even fraud claims to the 18-month period, AUD 25k de minimis, basket and 20% cap. It must be reversed: limitations apply **only** to general Warranty Claims, and expressly **not** to (a) fraud, dishonesty or wilful concealment, (b) fundamental warranties, (c) tax warranties/indemnity, (d) specific indemnities, (e) leakage/price-adjustment mechanics, (f) covenants to deliver Completion items. These carve-outs should be stated positively in the SPA, not left to inference.

### 2.2 Exclusive remedy and non-reliance (cl. 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

Applying exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions to "all Claims of any nature" is overreach. Points:

- **Fraud carve-out** is mandatory. A non-reliance clause cannot be used to shield fraudulent misrepresentation, and the SPA should say so expressly rather than relying on the courts.
- **Exclusive remedy** must not cut across specific indemnities, the tax indemnity, Completion-deliverable covenants, injunctive relief for breach of restraints/confidentiality, or the Buyer's termination rights.
- **Statutory claims.** Liability under s 18 ACL (misleading or deceptive conduct) cannot be contractually excluded; non-reliance clauses operate on reliance/causation, not on the cause of action. The clause should be drafted so it does not purport to exclude non-excludable statutory rights (otherwise it invites argument about severability of the whole clause).
- Non-reliance should be reciprocal and limited to pre-contractual statements *outside* the SPA, Disclosure Letter and Completion deliverables – the Buyer is plainly relying on the Disclosure Letter and on the data room materials the Seller itself is relying on for disclosure.

### 2.3 Disclosure (Schedule 7; Disclosure Letter paras 1.1–1.2, 11)

**General data-room disclosure.** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the data room, plus the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records," is the broadest form available. Position:

- Disclosure is only effective if **fairly disclosed** – with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and its likely effect. "Referred to in" should be deleted; a passing cross-reference is not disclosure.
- Delete general disclosure of public registers. ASIC and PPSR searches are a reasonable exception if confined to searches actually conducted and listed, with results annexed, as at a specified date.
- The data-room index should be annexed and the data room frozen (USB/hard copy) at the stated cut-off, so there is no argument later about what was "in" it.

**Cut-off date.** The Disclosure Letter speaks as at 5.00pm, 22 September 2026. It is now 4 November. The Seller must deliver an updated Disclosure Letter at signing, and we should resist any further disclosure against warranties repeated at Completion except for matters arising in the ordinary course between signing and Completion that are notified promptly – with a Buyer termination right if the new disclosure is material.

**Para 1.4 (no admissions) and para 11 (reservation).** Para 1.4 is conventional and acceptable. Para 11 is unusual: it effectively tells the Buyer to form its own view on everything and signals that the Seller will argue that any matter in the record was disclosed and knowable. It confirms why cl. 8.3 (below) has to go.

Note in our favour: the Disclosure Letter is unusually candid about what has *not* been done (no Bluefen consent, no Riverlark discharge, no Ironquay receipt/assignment, bonuses not in funds flow, DD-006 investigation preliminary). We should quote those admissions back in our mark-up.

### 2.4 Buyer knowledge (cl. 8.3) – reject

The clause bars claims for any matter of which the Buyer **or its advisers** had knowledge, including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records." This is a constructive-knowledge anti-sandbagging clause and is not acceptable:

- "Discoverable" means every matter touched on anywhere in the data room, or in any ASIC/PPSR/court record, is excluded regardless of whether it was actually understood – it swallows the fair-disclosure standard entirely.
- Extending it to advisers means the Seller can run arguments about what a DD lawyer or accountant "should have" picked up.
- It double-dips with general disclosure: the Seller gets disclosure protection *and* a knowledge bar.

Position: delete. Fallback: actual knowledge only, of a short named list of Buyer deal-team individuals, limited to matters where that individual was actually aware both of the facts and that they constituted a breach of warranty; no adviser imputation; no "discoverable" or "ought to have known" language.

### 2.5 Bluefen consent (cl. 3 / 6.3) – ~30% of revenue

The Update says the consent "is addressed." The Disclosure Letter says no final written consent and no evidence that the cl. 11.3 conditions have been satisfied. Treat as unaddressed.

Problems with the Seller's formulation:

- "Reasonable endeavours" is a low standard for a contract representing ~AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue. We need at minimum "all reasonable endeavours," and ideally a defined set of obligations (make the approach jointly with the Buyer, provide information, not agree to amended terms without Buyer consent).
- "Treat as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores cl. 11.3. If Bluefen's consent is conditional, a bare consent letter that leaves conditions unsatisfied does not protect the Company. The condition precedent must be: **unconditional written consent from Bluefen, in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, confirming that the cl. 11.3 conditions are satisfied or waived, and that Bluefen will not exercise any termination/renegotiation right arising from the change of control.**
- The CP should be for the Buyer's benefit only (waivable by Buyer alone), with a long-stop date and Buyer termination right.
- Residual protection: a specific indemnity or a retention/escrow (sized by reference to the gross margin on the contract) if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces scope within, say, 12 months of Completion on grounds connected to the change of control. Alternatively a price adjustment mechanism.

We should also confirm whether there are *other* material customer contracts with change-of-control triggers (Mossvale is addressed below, but the Disclosure Letter is silent on the rest of the customer book).

### 2.6 Riverlark facility (cl. 2 / 7) – ~AUD 3.2m

This is the clearest departure from the agreed basis. The deal is debt-free/cash-free at AUD 24m. The Seller proposes that a AUD 3.2m secured facility remains outstanding at Completion, with a release "to be provided following Completion." That means:

- The Buyer pays full price and acquires a company still carrying AUD 3.2m of debt and Riverlark's security over its assets. Unless the price is reduced, the Buyer pays for the debt twice.
- DD-003 cl. 8.1 (change of control) almost certainly makes Completion an event of default/mandatory prepayment event. Completing with the facility live exposes the Company to enforcement on day one.
- Riverlark's security may extend to the **shares** (a share mortgage or specific security over Harbourglass's shares is common in venture-backed structures). If so, the Seller cannot deliver clean title at Completion – which goes directly to the title point in 2.11.
- A post-Completion release relies on the Seller's covenant and the Seller's cash. Harbourglass is a venture vehicle; its post-Completion covenant strength is unknown.

Position: the facility is Debt and is deducted from the price or, more cleanly, repaid at Completion **out of the purchase price** by direct payment to Riverlark under the funds flow. Completion deliverables must include a payoff letter from Riverlark (stating the exact payout figure and confirming release on receipt), executed deeds of release/discharge of all security, PPSR financing-change statements/releases and any share-mortgage discharge, delivered in escrow on the day. Completion should not occur without them. If the Seller resists, it is a condition precedent.

Separately, PPSR searches against the Company and Harbourglass should be refreshed immediately to see what Riverlark (and anyone else) has registered.

### 2.7 Completion bonuses (DD-005) – AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller" but they are not in the funds flow and there is no indication the Seller will fund them. The bonuses are payable by **the Company** to its employees, triggered by Completion, with continued-employment conditions – i.e. they crystallise *after* the Buyer owns the Company. Unless addressed, the Buyer funds them.

Additional points:

- On-costs are not addressed: superannuation (12% SG rate) and NSW payroll tax (5.45%) on AUD 420,000 add roughly AUD 75–80k, and there may be PAYG withholding timing/cash-flow effects. Total exposure is likely AUD 500,000+.
- The "continued-employment" condition could mean the Buyer must keep paying out over a retention period; if an employee leaves, the condition fails but that is cold comfort if the Buyer wanted the employee.
- If any bonuses are payable to Seller-nominated directors or related parties, that is leakage.

Position: treat the bonuses and all associated on-costs as **Transaction Costs / Debt** in the price definition, deducted from the Completion payment or (if a locked-box) treated as leakage; alternatively the Seller funds the Company with the full gross-up amount at Completion, shown as a line in the funds flow. The Seller should warrant and indemnify for any other transaction bonuses, change-of-control payments or retention arrangements not disclosed.

### 2.8 Ironquay IP (cl. 11.1) – indemnity "limited to the SOW3 payment" is inadequate

This is a title-to-IP issue, not a payables issue. Under DD-004 cl. 7.3, the SOW3 Project Materials transfer to the Company **only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open; there is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment. On the documents, the Company does not currently own the SOW3 deliverables – and Ironquay, as developer, holds the copyright until payment.

The Seller's indemnity for "the specific SOW3 payment" covers AUD 180,000. The actual exposure is: inability to use, licence or sell products incorporating SOW3 materials; infringement claims by Ironquay; re-development cost; customer disruption; and, if SOW3 materials are embedded in what Bluefen or Mossvale receive, a chain of downstream problems.

Position:

- **Completion deliverable / CP:** evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (paid by the Seller, or deducted from price and paid at Completion via the funds flow), *and* an executed confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay to the Company of all SOW3 Project Materials (including moral-rights consents and source code/documentation delivery), plus a release confirming no further amounts owing.
- **Indemnity:** broadened to all Loss arising from any failure of the Company to have full title to IP created under any Ironquay SOW, uncapped or subject to a separate high cap, outside the general time limit, and expressly outside the cl. 12.3 sweeper.
- **Warranty:** that the Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business and that all contractors have assigned developed IP – not subject to the general cap, per 2.1.
- DD should check whether SOW1 and SOW2 had the same conditional-transfer mechanic and whether those fees are fully paid.

### 2.9 Export/privacy incident (DD-006) – "not expected to be material" is the Seller's characterisation, not a fact

The Disclosure Letter is clear that the investigation is preliminary and that the Seller cannot say whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, what the exact scope is, or whether notification is required. ~1,240 records containing names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps is personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Issues:

- **Notifiable Data Breaches scheme.** Once an entity suspects an eligible data breach, it must carry out a reasonable and expeditious assessment within 30 days. The incident was in the data room by 22 September; 30 days has passed. If the assessment has not been completed, the Company is likely already non-compliant. If the breach is "likely to result in serious harm," OAIC and affected-individual notification is required. Civil penalties for serious/repeated interferences with privacy are now very substantial (up to the greater of AUD 50m, 3× benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover).
- **Contractual exposure.** If the records relate to a customer's personnel or end-users (activity timestamps suggest platform data – possibly Bluefen's or Mossvale's), there are likely contractual notification obligations and potential customer claims, and this could feed into the Bluefen consent discussion.
- **Disclosure defeats warranty.** Because the incident is disclosed, data-protection warranties won't help. Protection has to be an indemnity.

Position: (a) pre-signing covenant that the Seller procures completion of the NDB assessment and any required OAIC/individual/customer notifications before Completion, with the Buyer given access to the investigation report and a say on notification; (b) a specific indemnity for all Loss arising from the DD-006 incident (regulatory, remediation, customer claims, notification costs), uncapped or separately capped, outside the general time limit and sweeper; (c) warranty that, other than DD-006, there have been no data breaches or regulatory contact, and that the Company has a compliant privacy programme.

### 2.10 Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008 / DD-011) – AUD 330,000

The Seller calls these "ordinary course." The Disclosure Letter itself says it does **not** state whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course – so the Seller's cover-note characterisation has no support in the disclosure. Points:

- Three "related" contracts at exactly AUD 110,000 each is a pattern worth probing: is this one arrangement split into three (e.g. to sit below internal approval thresholds, or to fall below a materiality threshold in the SPA)? Is Sandbar a related party of the Seller or management?
- If the renewals are committed pre-Completion but not accrued in the Accounts or reflected in working capital, they are either debt-like items or a working-capital adjustment.

Position: request the contracts and renewal notices; confirm accrual treatment; confirm no related-party connection; if committed and unaccrued, treat as Debt/working-capital deduction; ensure the SPA aggregates related claims for de minimis purposes so this structure cannot be used to defeat a claim.

### 2.11 Title to shares – do not rely on the share register alone

The Seller says title is "evidenced by" the DD-012 share register, and the Disclosure Letter expressly notes the Buyer has not completed its own verification. The register is prima facie evidence only. Before signing we should: run current ASIC company and Harbourglass searches; PPSR search against Harbourglass for security over the Paperbark shares (see Riverlark, 2.6); review the constitution and any shareholders' agreement for pre-emptive rights, drag/tag or consent requirements; confirm issued capital, no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP interests (a venture-backed analytics company very commonly has an ESOP – its absence from the disclosure is notable); and check the share certificates and any share transfer history. Title warranty: fundamental, 100% cap, long period, per 2.1.

### 2.12 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) – lower risk, but tidy up

- **Lease:** a notification obligation is manageable, but make compliance a pre-Completion Seller covenant and confirm there is no change-of-control or "deemed assignment" provision elsewhere in the lease, and no landlord guarantee from Harbourglass that would need replacing.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not bite on a share sale, as the Seller says, but we should confirm the contract contains no separate change-of-control clause and that the Mossvale contract is not affected by DD-006 or the Ironquay IP issue.

### 2.13 Seller covenant strength

Harbourglass is a venture vehicle. Every protection above (indemnities, post-Completion releases, bonus funding) is only as good as the Seller's ability to pay after it has distributed proceeds. Position: a retention/escrow (say 10–15% for 18–24 months, plus specific escrows for Bluefen and DD-006 if those remain unresolved), and/or a parent/fund guarantee, and/or W&I insurance with the Seller bearing part of the premium.

## 3. Summary of recommendations

**Must-haves (walk-away level if not addressed):**

1. **Riverlark:** facility repaid at Completion from the purchase price via the funds flow; payoff letter, deeds of release and PPSR/share-security discharges delivered at Completion. Not post-Completion.
2. **Fundamental, tax and IP warranties carved out** of the 20%/18-month regime: title/capacity at 100% of price for 6–7 years; tax indemnity 7 years at 100%; IP warranties at an elevated cap and longer period.
3. **Delete the cl. 12.3 sweeper** and expressly carve fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, leakage and Completion covenants out of all limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions.
4. **Delete cl. 8.3** (constructive knowledge). Fallback: actual knowledge of named individuals only, no adviser imputation, no "discoverable."
5. **Bluefen:** CP of unconditional consent satisfactory to the Buyer with cl. 11.3 conditions evidenced as satisfied; Buyer-only waiver; long-stop; indemnity/escrow for post-Completion loss of the contract.
6. **Ironquay:** payment of all SOW3 fees and confirmatory IP assignment as Completion deliverables; indemnity broadened to all IP-title loss, outside caps and sweeper.

**Strong pushes:**

7. **Bonuses:** AUD 420k plus super/payroll tax treated as Transaction Costs/Debt deducted from price or Seller-funded at Completion and itemised in the funds flow; warranty/indemnity for any other change-of-control payments.
8. **DD-006:** NDB assessment and any notifications completed pre-Completion; specific uncapped (or separately capped) indemnity; Buyer access to the investigation.
9. **Disclosure:** fair-disclosure standard; delete "referred to in" and general public-register disclosure; data room frozen and indexed; updated Disclosure Letter at signing; limited disclosure against Completion warranties with Buyer termination right for material new matters.
10. **Thresholds:** tipping basket; de minimis AUD 10–15k; aggregation of related claims.
11. **Sandbar:** obtain the contracts, confirm accrual and related-party status; treat committed unaccrued amounts as Debt/working capital.
12. **Security for claims:** retention/escrow and/or guarantee and/or W&I.

**Negotiable:**

13. General cap: open at 30–50%, likely land in the 20–30% range once carve-outs secured; 18 months acceptable for general warranties only (24 months preferable).

**DD actions before we respond:** refresh ASIC/PPSR searches on the Company and Harbourglass (looking specifically for share security); confirm no ESOP/options/convertibles; obtain Bluefen cl. 11.3 conditions, the Sandbar contracts, SOW1–2 payment status, and the current state of the DD-006 investigation.

**Framing for the response letter:** lead with the inconsistency between the Seller Update's "addressed/adequate/settled/not material" language and the Disclosure Letter's own admissions that nothing has been resolved. The Seller has conceded the facts; our mark-up simply follows them through to their proper allocation under a debt-free/cash-free deal.

2. **Neutralise warranties through disclosure** – general disclosure of the whole data room and public registers, plus a constructive-knowledge bar (cl. 8.3) that would defeat claims on anything "discoverable."
3. **Leave known, quantified liabilities in the Company** post-Completion while taking a price struck on a debt-free/cash-free basis.

Items 1 and 2 together mean that for the known problems (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonuses, DD-006, Sandbar) a warranty claim would be essentially impossible: they are disclosed, so warranties don't bite; they are "discoverable," so cl. 8.3 bars them; and even if a claim survived, the cap/basket/time limits apply. Those matters therefore have to be dealt with by **price, Completion deliverables, conditions and specific indemnities**, not warranties.

Roughly quantified, the identified items the Seller is proposing to leave with the Company or unaddressed are:

| Item | Amount | Seller's proposal | Effect on debt-free/cash-free price |
|---|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility | ~AUD 3,200,000 | Release "following Completion" | Buyer effectively pays this twice |
| DD-005 completion bonuses | AUD 420,000 + on-costs (super, payroll tax) ~AUD 500,000+ | Not in funds flow; "matter for Seller" | Company pays post-Completion |
| Ironquay SOW3 fee | AUD 180,000 (+ IP not yet vested) | Indemnity for the fee only | IP title risk unpriced |
| Sandbar renewals | AUD 330,000 | "Ordinary course" | Possibly unaccrued committed cost |
| **Total** | **~AUD 4.2m+ (c. 17% of price)** | | |

Plus unquantified exposure on Bluefen (~30% of revenue) and the DD-006 privacy incident.

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### 2.1 Liability regime (cl. 12.1–12.3, 13) – reject the "one regime for everything" approach

**Cap (20% / AUD 4.8m).** A 20% general-warranty cap is at the low end but within range for an Australian mid-market private deal; it is negotiable rather than unacceptable *provided* it applies only to general business warranties. We should open at a higher figure (30–50%) and may ultimately accept something in the 20–30% range if the carve-outs below are secured. Note also that if we take W&I insurance, the cap debate changes shape – worth raising with the brokers now.

**Fundamental/title warranties.** The Seller's proposal to subject capacity and title warranties to the same cap and 18-month limit "for administrative simplicity" is not market and must be rejected. If title to the shares fails, the Buyer has paid AUD 24m for nothing; a AUD 4.8m recovery capped at 18 months is no remedy. Position: fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, no insolvency, share capital) at 100% of price, with a 6–7 year (or statutory limitation) claim period, outside the de minimis and basket.

**Tax.** The Seller says tax is "settled under the general regime." It is not. ATO amendment periods run 4 years from assessment in most cases (longer for fraud/evasion and certain matters), so an 18-month window leaves the Buyer exposed for most of the audit period. Position: tax warranties and a stand-alone tax indemnity with a 7-year period, cap at 100% of price (or at minimum well above the general cap), not subject to disclosure, de minimis or basket.

**IP.** For an analytics business, IP is the asset. Given the known Ironquay defect (see 2.6), IP warranties should sit at an elevated cap (at least 50%, ideally 100%) with a longer period (e.g. 3–4 years), and should not be swept into the 18-month/20% regime.

**Thresholds.** De minimis of AUD 25,000 (~0.1%) is at the top of the usual range; AUD 10–15k is more typical for this deal size. Basket of AUD 250,000 (~1%) is market, but it should be a **tipping** basket (recover from the first dollar once exceeded), not excess-only. Related claims arising from the same facts should aggregate for de minimis purposes – the Sandbar structure (three contracts of AUD 110k each) shows exactly why.

**The "sweeper" (cl. 12.3 second sentence).** "Any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" is the most dangerous single line in the Update. On its face it subjects the Ironquay indemnity, any tax indemnity, leakage claims, completion-accounts adjustments, and even fraud claims to the 18-month period, AUD 25k de minimis, basket and 20% cap. It must be reversed: limitations apply **only** to general Warranty Claims, and expressly **not** to (a) fraud, dishonesty or wilful concealment, (b) fundamental warranties, (c) tax warranties/indemnity, (d) specific indemnities, (e) leakage/price-adjustment mechanics, (f) covenants to deliver Completion items. These carve-outs should be stated positively in the SPA, not left to inference.

### 2.2 Exclusive remedy and non-reliance (cl. 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

Applying exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions to "all Claims of any nature" is overreach. Points:

- **Fraud carve-out** is mandatory. A non-reliance clause cannot be used to shield fraudulent misrepresentation, and the SPA should say so expressly rather than relying on the courts.
- **Exclusive remedy** must not cut across specific indemnities, the tax indemnity, Completion-deliverable covenants, injunctive relief for breach of restraints/confidentiality, or the Buyer's termination rights.
- **Statutory claims.** Liability under s 18 ACL (misleading or deceptive conduct) cannot be contractually excluded; non-reliance clauses operate on reliance/causation, not on the cause of action. The clause should be drafted so it does not purport to exclude non-excludable statutory rights (otherwise it invites argument about severability of the whole clause).
- Non-reliance should be reciprocal and limited to pre-contractual statements *outside* the SPA, Disclosure Letter and Completion deliverables – the Buyer is plainly relying on the Disclosure Letter and on the data room materials the Seller itself is relying on for disclosure.

### 2.3 Disclosure (Schedule 7; Disclosure Letter paras 1.1–1.2, 11)

**General data-room disclosure.** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the data room, plus the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records," is the broadest form available. Position:

- Disclosure is only effective if **fairly disclosed** – with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and its likely effect. "Referred to in" should be deleted; a passing cross-reference is not disclosure.
- Delete general disclosure of public registers. ASIC and PPSR searches are a reasonable exception if confined to searches actually conducted and listed, with results annexed, as at a specified date.
- The data-room index should be annexed and the data room frozen (USB/hard copy) at the stated cut-off, so there is no argument later about what was "in" it.

**Cut-off date.** The Disclosure Letter speaks as at 5.00pm, 22 September 2026. It is now 4 November. The Seller must deliver an updated Disclosure Letter at signing, and we should resist any further disclosure against warranties repeated at Completion except for matters arising in the ordinary course between signing and Completion that are notified promptly – with a Buyer termination right if the new disclosure is material.

**Para 1.4 (no admissions) and para 11 (reservation).** Para 1.4 is conventional and acceptable. Para 11 is unusual: it effectively tells the Buyer to form its own view on everything and signals that the Seller will argue that any matter in the record was disclosed and knowable. It confirms why cl. 8.3 (below) has to go.

Note in our favour: the Disclosure Letter is unusually candid about what has *not* been done (no Bluefen consent, no Riverlark discharge, no Ironquay receipt/assignment, bonuses not in funds flow, DD-006 investigation preliminary). We should quote those admissions back in our mark-up.

### 2.4 Buyer knowledge (cl. 8.3) – reject

The clause bars claims for any matter of which the Buyer **or its advisers** had knowledge, including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records." This is a constructive-knowledge anti-sandbagging clause and is not acceptable:

- "Discoverable" means every matter touched on anywhere in the data room, or in any ASIC/PPSR/court record, is excluded regardless of whether it was actually understood – it swallows the fair-disclosure standard entirely.
- Extending it to advisers means the Seller can run arguments about what a DD lawyer or accountant "should have" picked up.
- It double-dips with general disclosure: the Seller gets disclosure protection *and* a knowledge bar.

Position: delete. Fallback: actual knowledge only, of a short named list of Buyer deal-team individuals, limited to matters where that individual was actually aware both of the facts and that they constituted a breach of warranty; no adviser imputation; no "discoverable" or "ought to have known" language.

### 2.5 Bluefen consent (cl. 3 / 6.3) – ~30% of revenue

The Update says the consent "is addressed." The Disclosure Letter says no final written consent and no evidence that the cl. 11.3 conditions have been satisfied. Treat as unaddressed.

Problems with the Seller's formulation:

- "Reasonable endeavours" is a low standard for a contract representing ~AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue. We need at minimum "all reasonable endeavours," and ideally a defined set of obligations (make the approach jointly with the Buyer, provide information, not agree to amended terms without Buyer consent).
- "Treat as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores cl. 11.3. If Bluefen's consent is conditional, a bare consent letter that leaves conditions unsatisfied does not protect the Company. The condition precedent must be: **unconditional written consent from Bluefen, in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, confirming that the cl. 11.3 conditions are satisfied or waived, and that Bluefen will not exercise any termination/renegotiation right arising from the change of control.**
- The CP should be for the Buyer's benefit only (waivable by Buyer alone), with a long-stop date and Buyer termination right.
- Residual protection: a specific indemnity or a retention/escrow (sized by reference to the gross margin on the contract) if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces scope within, say, 12 months of Completion on grounds connected to the change of control. Alternatively a price adjustment mechanism.

We should also confirm whether there are *other* material customer contracts with change-of-control triggers (Mossvale is addressed below, but the Disclosure Letter is silent on the rest of the customer book).

### 2.6 Riverlark facility (cl. 2 / 7) – ~AUD 3.2m

This is the clearest departure from the agreed basis. The deal is debt-free/cash-free at AUD 24m. The Seller proposes that a AUD 3.2m secured facility remains outstanding at Completion, with a release "to be provided following Completion." That means:

- The Buyer pays full price and acquires a company still carrying AUD 3.2m of debt and Riverlark's security over its assets. Unless the price is reduced, the Buyer pays for the debt twice.
- DD-003 cl. 8.1 (change of control) almost certainly makes Completion an event of default/mandatory prepayment event. Completing with the facility live exposes the Company to enforcement on day one.
- Riverlark's security may extend to the **shares** (a share mortgage or specific security over Harbourglass's shares is common in venture-backed structures). If so, the Seller cannot deliver clean title at Completion – which goes directly to the title point in 2.11.
- A post-Completion release relies on the Seller's covenant and the Seller's cash. Harbourglass is a venture vehicle; its post-Completion covenant strength is unknown.

Position: the facility is Debt and is deducted from the price or, more cleanly, repaid at Completion **out of the purchase price** by direct payment to Riverlark under the funds flow. Completion deliverables must include a payoff letter from Riverlark (stating the exact payout figure and confirming release on receipt), executed deeds of release/discharge of all security, PPSR financing-change statements/releases and any share-mortgage discharge, delivered in escrow on the day. Completion should not occur without them. If the Seller resists, it is a condition precedent.

Separately, PPSR searches against the Company and Harbourglass should be refreshed immediately to see what Riverlark (and anyone else) has registered.

### 2.7 Completion bonuses (DD-005) – AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller" but they are not in the funds flow and there is no indication the Seller will fund them. The bonuses are payable by **the Company** to its employees, triggered by Completion, with continued-employment conditions – i.e. they crystallise *after* the Buyer owns the Company. Unless addressed, the Buyer funds them.

Additional points:

- On-costs are not addressed: superannuation (12% SG rate) and NSW payroll tax (5.45%) on AUD 420,000 add roughly AUD 75–80k, and there may be PAYG withholding timing/cash-flow effects. Total exposure is likely AUD 500,000+.
- The "continued-employment" condition could mean the Buyer must keep paying out over a retention period; if an employee leaves, the condition fails but that is cold comfort if the Buyer wanted the employee.
- If any bonuses are payable to Seller-nominated directors or related parties, that is leakage.

Position: treat the bonuses and all associated on-costs as **Transaction Costs / Debt** in the price definition, deducted from the Completion payment or (if a locked-box) treated as leakage; alternatively the Seller funds the Company with the full gross-up amount at Completion, shown as a line in the funds flow. The Seller should warrant and indemnify for any other transaction bonuses, change-of-control payments or retention arrangements not disclosed.

### 2.8 Ironquay IP (cl. 11.1) – indemnity "limited to the SOW3 payment" is inadequate

This is a title-to-IP issue, not a payables issue. Under DD-004 cl. 7.3, the SOW3 Project Materials transfer to the Company **only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open; there is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment. On the documents, the Company does not currently own the SOW3 deliverables – and Ironquay, as developer, holds the copyright until payment.

The Seller's indemnity for "the specific SOW3 payment" covers AUD 180,000. The actual exposure is: inability to use, licence or sell products incorporating SOW3 materials; infringement claims by Ironquay; re-development cost; customer disruption; and, if SOW3 materials are embedded in what Bluefen or Mossvale receive, a chain of downstream problems.

Position:

- **Completion deliverable / CP:** evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (paid by the Seller, or deducted from price and paid at Completion via the funds flow), *and* an executed confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay to the Company of all SOW3 Project Materials (including moral-rights consents and source code/documentation delivery), plus a release confirming no further amounts owing.
- **Indemnity:** broadened to all Loss arising from any failure of the Company to have full title to IP created under any Ironquay SOW, uncapped or subject to a separate high cap, outside the general time limit, and expressly outside the cl. 12.3 sweeper.
- **Warranty:** that the Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business and that all contractors have assigned developed IP – not subject to the general cap, per 2.1.
- DD should check whether SOW1 and SOW2 had the same conditional-transfer mechanic and whether those fees are fully paid.

### 2.9 Export/privacy incident (DD-006) – "not expected to be material" is the Seller's characterisation, not a fact

The Disclosure Letter is clear that the investigation is preliminary and that the Seller cannot say whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, what the exact scope is, or whether notification is required. ~1,240 records containing names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps is personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Issues:

- **Notifiable Data Breaches scheme.** Once an entity suspects an eligible data breach, it must carry out a reasonable and expeditious assessment within 30 days. The incident was in the data room by 22 September; 30 days has passed. If the assessment has not been completed, the Company is likely already non-compliant. If the breach is "likely to result in serious harm," OAIC and affected-individual notification is required. Civil penalties for serious/repeated interferences with privacy are now very substantial (up to the greater of AUD 50m, 3× benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover).
- **Contractual exposure.** If the records relate to a customer's personnel or end-users (activity timestamps suggest platform data – possibly Bluefen's or Mossvale's), there are likely contractual notification obligations and potential customer claims, and this could feed into the Bluefen consent discussion.
- **Disclosure defeats warranty.** Because the incident is disclosed, data-protection warranties won't help. Protection has to be an indemnity.

Position: (a) pre-signing covenant that the Seller procures completion of the NDB assessment and any required OAIC/individual/customer notifications before Completion, with the Buyer given access to the investigation report and a say on notification; (b) a specific indemnity for all Loss arising from the DD-006 incident (regulatory, remediation, customer claims, notification costs), uncapped or separately capped, outside the general time limit and sweeper; (c) warranty that, other than DD-006, there have been no data breaches or regulatory contact, and that the Company has a compliant privacy programme.

### 2.10 Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008 / DD-011) – AUD 330,000

The Seller calls these "ordinary course." The Disclosure Letter itself says it does **not** state whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course – so the Seller's cover-note characterisation has no support in the disclosure. Points:

- Three "related" contracts at exactly AUD 110,000 each is a pattern worth probing: is this one arrangement split into three (e.g. to sit below internal approval thresholds, or to fall below a materiality threshold in the SPA)? Is Sandbar a related party of the Seller or management?
- If the renewals are committed pre-Completion but not accrued in the Accounts or reflected in working capital, they are either debt-like items or a working-capital adjustment.

Position: request the contracts and renewal notices; confirm accrual treatment; confirm no related-party connection; if committed and unaccrued, treat as Debt/working-capital deduction; ensure the SPA aggregates related claims for de minimis purposes so this structure cannot be used to defeat a claim.

### 2.11 Title to shares – do not rely on the share register alone

The Seller says title is "evidenced by" the DD-012 share register, and the Disclosure Letter expressly notes the Buyer has not completed its own verification. The register is prima facie evidence only. Before signing we should: run current ASIC company and Harbourglass searches; PPSR search against Harbourglass for security over the Paperbark shares (see Riverlark, 2.6); review the constitution and any shareholders' agreement for pre-emptive rights, drag/tag or consent requirements; confirm issued capital, no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP interests (a venture-backed analytics company very commonly has an ESOP – its absence from the disclosure is notable); and check the share certificates and any share transfer history. Title warranty: fundamental, 100% cap, long period, per 2.1.

### 2.12 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) – lower risk, but tidy up

- **Lease:** a notification obligation is manageable, but make compliance a pre-Completion Seller covenant and confirm there is no change-of-control or "deemed assignment" provision elsewhere in the lease, and no landlord guarantee from Harbourglass that would need replacing.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not bite on a share sale, as the Seller says, but we should confirm the contract contains no separate change-of-control clause and that the Mossvale contract is not affected by DD-006 or the Ironquay IP issue.

### 2.13 Seller covenant strength

Harbourglass is a venture vehicle. Every protection above (indemnities, post-Completion releases, bonus funding) is only as good as the Seller's ability to pay after it has distributed proceeds. Position: a retention/escrow (say 10–15% for 18–24 months, plus specific escrows for Bluefen and DD-006 if those remain unresolved), and/or a parent/fund guarantee, and/or W&I insurance with the Seller bearing part of the premium.

## 3. Summary of recommendations

**Must-haves (walk-away level if not addressed):**

1. **Riverlark:** facility repaid at Completion from the purchase price via the funds flow; payoff letter, deeds of release and PPSR/share-security discharges delivered at Completion. Not post-Completion.
2. **Fundamental, tax and IP warranties carved out** of the 20%/18-month regime: title/capacity at 100% of price for 6–7 years; tax indemnity 7 years at 100%; IP warranties at an elevated cap and longer period.
3. **Delete the cl. 12.3 sweeper** and expressly carve fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, leakage and Completion covenants out of all limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions.
4. **Delete cl. 8.3** (constructive knowledge). Fallback: actual knowledge of named individuals only, no adviser imputation, no "discoverable."
5. **Bluefen:** CP of unconditional consent satisfactory to the Buyer with cl. 11.3 conditions evidenced as satisfied; Buyer-only waiver; long-stop; indemnity/escrow for post-Completion loss of the contract.
6. **Ironquay:** payment of all SOW3 fees and confirmatory IP assignment as Completion deliverables; indemnity broadened to all IP-title loss, outside caps and sweeper.

**Strong pushes:**

7. **Bonuses:** AUD 420k plus super/payroll tax treated as Transaction Costs/Debt deducted from price or Seller-funded at Completion and itemised in the funds flow; warranty/indemnity for any other change-of-control payments.
8. **DD-006:** NDB assessment and any notifications completed pre-Completion; specific uncapped (or separately capped) indemnity; Buyer access to the investigation.
9. **Disclosure:** fair-disclosure standard; delete "referred to in" and general public-register disclosure; data room frozen and indexed; updated Disclosure Letter at signing; limited disclosure against Completion warranties with Buyer termination right for material new matters.
10. **Thresholds:** tipping basket; de minimis AUD 10–15k; aggregation of related claims.
11. **Sandbar:** obtain the contracts, confirm accrual and related-party status; treat committed unaccrued amounts as Debt/working capital.
12. **Security for claims:** retention/escrow and/or guarantee and/or W&I.

**Negotiable:**

13. General cap: open at 30–50%, likely land in the 20–30% range once carve-outs secured; 18 months acceptable for general warranties only (24 months preferable).

**DD actions before we respond:** refresh ASIC/PPSR searches on the Company and Harbourglass (looking specifically for share security); confirm no ESOP/options/convertibles; obtain Bluefen cl. 11.3 conditions, the Sandbar contracts, SOW1–2 payment status, and the current state of the DD-006 investigation.

**Framing for the response letter:** lead with the inconsistency between the Seller Update's "addressed/adequate/settled/not material" language and the Disclosure Letter's own admissions that nothing has been resolved. The Seller has conceded the facts; our mark-up simply follows them through to their proper allocation under a debt-free/cash-free deal.
